In Ex Circum

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and see where the halfway points between its centre and its three outside centres land.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press Show claim and Check midpoints to see what always stays true.
Look for the math

The centre inside a triangle and the three centres outside it look far apart. Yet the dots halfway along the segments that join them keep landing on the circle drawn through the three corners. Here is why that is not luck.

A triangle hidden outside the first one

Each angle bisector of ABC is perpendicular to the outside bisector at the same corner. The outside bisectors meet at the three excenters Ia, Ib, Ic, forming the excentral triangle. Press Show bisectors to see the six right angles, and Show angle marks for the matching pairs of angles.

The sides of that outer triangle pass through A, B and C at right angles to the lines from its vertices, so ABC is its orthic triangle. The incenter I is the outer triangle's orthocentre.

One circle does two jobs

A nine-point circle passes through three feet of altitudes, three side midpoints and three Euler points. For the outer triangle these are A, B, C; the midpoints of IaIb, IbIc, IcIa; and the midpoints from its orthocentre I to its vertices. The last three are exactly

Ma = (I + Ia) / 2,   Mb = (I + Ib) / 2,   Mc = (I + Ic) / 2.

That circle is also the circumcircle of ABC, so all three halfway dots lie on it. The logic test checks this and the other named points on hundreds of triangles: all hold.

The arc midpoints, and the source

There is more: each dot is also the midpoint of the arc of the circumcircle that its segment crosses. For example Ma is equally far from B, C, I and Ia. The check script constructs those arc midpoints a second way — as the circle through the opposite side and I — and confirms the page's extra claim throughout.

The live cut-the-knot page no longer embeds the Java applet; an archived 2018 capture shows a GeoGebra sketch in its place. This port takes its construction from the original InExCircum bytecode and its written claim from that same page: the midpoints of the segments joining the incenter to the excenters lie on the circumcircle.

Try pulling one corner so the triangle is long and thin: the outside centres fly away, but the halfway dots still sit on the circle.
